title: Zero Registered Slaughterhouses: Vietnam's Dog Meat Trade Has No Safety Net
excerpt: Vietnam's dog meat trade operates in a complete regulatory vacuum. Here's what that means for public health — and how other countries fixed it.
body_html:
Every year, an estimated 5 million dogs are killed for meat in Vietnam. Not one of the facilities handling this trade is registered, inspected, or held to any food safety standard. In a country with robust regulations governing pork, poultry, and seafood, this gap is not an oversight — it is a structural failure with real consequences for the Vietnamese public.

The absence of registered slaughterhouses means there is no veterinary inspection at the point of slaughter, no cold-chain verification, no testing for pathogens, and no traceability if an outbreak occurs. Dogs entering this supply chain are frequently transported in overcrowded, unsanitary conditions across provincial and national borders — a documented pathway for rabies transmission, as well as contamination by E. coli and Salmonella. Rabies, a near-universally fatal disease once symptoms appear, remains endemic in Vietnam, and the unregulated movement of dogs for slaughter directly undermines national eradication efforts.

The international evidence is instructive. South Korea, which operated a similarly unregulated dog meat industry for decades, saw measurable improvements in food safety compliance and zoonotic disease surveillance following targeted regulatory intervention that ultimately accelerated a broader legislative ban. The Philippines enacted a full ban in 1998 under its Animal Welfare Act; enforcement gaps persisted, but the legal framework empowered local authorities and health agencies to act. In both cases, reform was driven not by external pressure alone, but by domestic public health advocates and citizens who had already shifted in values.

That domestic shift is precisely what has happened in Vietnam. A 2021 survey found that 95% of Vietnamese people support ending the dog meat trade — a figure that reflects changing urban attitudes, generational shifts, and a growing awareness of the health risks involved. Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City have both issued non-binding guidance encouraging the trade's end. What is missing is the legislative architecture to match public will with enforceable policy. Regulation is not the ceiling of ambition here — it is the floor. Mandatory registration of any facility handling dog meat for sale would immediately expose the scale of the problem and create accountability. Mandatory veterinary inspection would either bring the trade into compliance with standards applied to every other meat — a standard it cannot realistically meet — or accelerate its closure.

Lucky, a nine-year-old Vietnamese Tả dog, represents the millions of family companions who enter this supply chain through theft and illegal transport, with no traceability and no recourse for the families they are taken from. The regulatory vacuum does not only harm animals — it harms the Vietnamese families and communities who deserve a food system they can trust. The 95% of Vietnamese who want this trade to end are not waiting for foreign instruction. They are waiting for a legal framework that reflects their own values. Add your voice to theirs and sign the petition today: https://www.change.org/p/end-dog-meat-trade-vietnam.
